items.name: narration_en
items.direction: Narrate this as a high-energy, feel-good geography story for BHUGOL, a popular geography fun-facts YouTube channel. The Narrator is thrilled to be telling you this: enthusiastic, upbeat, bright and very expressive, like an excited friend who can't wait to show you something amazing. Big smile in the voice the whole way. Wide, lively pitch movement: rise with real curiosity on every question, hit 'Small problem.' and 'Just seals.' with playful delight after a tiny comic pause, and say every number with genuine amazement, as if it surprises you too. Say '...they moved the border.' with a tiny deadpan pause before 'they moved the border', and 'All two metres of it.' as a dry aside. Land each punchline with a grin. Read numbers naturally. The last line trails off unfinished on 'at once...', voice staying up, so it can loop straight back into the first line. Pace is quick and bouncy, about 170 words per minute, with short crisp pauses; never slow, flat, calm, sleepy or documentary-serious. Accent: native General American English narrator, neutral American accent from the first word to the last. VOICE IDENTITY: always the same warm baritone host, same person and same energy level from the first line to the last. Pronounce 'Märket' as 'MAIR-ket'.
lines: Stand on this rock, and you're in two countries and two time zones at once.
One step, and your clock jumps an hour.
Half is Sweden, half is Finland. And the border? It zigzags like it had way too much coffee.
This is Märket: three hundred and fifty metres of bare rock. No trees, no people. Just seals.
Rewind to eighteen-oh-nine. Sweden loses Finland to the Russian Empire.
The new border? A straight line, right through this rock.
Then, in eighteen eighty-five, Finland builds a lighthouse on the highest point. All two metres of it.
Small problem. That point was in Sweden.
The lighthouse? It just liked the view.
And there it stood, in the wrong country, for one hundred years.
And the fix is even weirder.
In nineteen eighty-five, instead of moving the lighthouse... they moved the border.
Now the border bends around the tower in a four-hundred-and-eighty-metre S.
Finland keeps the lighthouse, and Sweden gets the same area back.
But remember, Sweden runs one hour behind Finland.
So zigzag across that line, and you hop back and forth in time.
Sweden's reward? An extra hour of sleep.
So next time someone says you can't be in two places at once...
